clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant familial primary aldosteronism associated with gain-of-function mutations in CLCN2, encoding the chloride channel ClC-2 in adrenal glomerulosa cells
Unlike type 1, it is not glucocorticoid-remediable, so aldosterone excess is not suppressed by dexamethasone and hybrid steroids are not the diagnostic hallmark
It presents as familial hypertension from primary aldosteronism, which may be due to adrenal hyperplasia, adenoma, or both, and can appear in childhood or adulthood
Biochemistry mirrors other primary aldosteronism with a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio and suppressed renin, with variable hypokalaemia
Diagnosis is clinical and biochemical, supported by CLCN2 testing and by excluding the chimeric gene of type 1; family screening is important
Management follows primary aldosteronism principles: mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists for bilateral disease and adrenalectomy for a lateralised aldosterone-producing lesion
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hyperaldosteronism type 2 is linked to germline gain-of-function variants in CLCN2, which encodes the voltage-gated chloride channel ClC-2 expressed in adrenal zona glomerulosa cells. Increased chloride efflux through the mutant channel depolarises the glomerulosa cell membrane, opening voltage-gated calcium channels and raising intracellular calcium, the key signal driving aldosterone synthase expression and aldosterone secretion. This produces autonomous, renin-independent aldosterone excess with sodium retention, volume expansion, and hypertension. Because the mechanism is independent of ACTH, the condition is not glucocorticoid-remediable, in contrast to the chimeric-gene disorder of type 1.
additionalDifferentials: Familial hyperaldosteronism types III (KCNJ5) and IV (CACNA1H)
Other monogenic hypertension syndromes (Liddle syndrome, apparent mineralocorticoid excess)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio with suppressed renin and confirmatory aldosterone testing
CLCN2 gene sequencing and exclusion of the type 1 chimeric gene
Adrenal cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) to identify adenoma or hyperplasia
Adrenal venous sampling to assess lateralisation before considering surgery
Absence of glucocorticoid-suppressible aldosterone and of type 1 hybrid steroids
redFlags: Early-onset or resistant hypertension with a strong family history
Significant hypokalaemia or its complications when present
Hypertensive end-organ damage at a young age
Lateralising lesion on venous sampling indicating a surgically curable cause
reference.prognosis: With diagnosis and targeted treatment, whether medical therapy for bilateral disease or surgery for a lateralised lesion, blood pressure and cardiovascular risk can be well controlled, whereas undiagnosed aldosterone excess drives hypertensive and cardiovascular complications. Outcome depends on early detection and family screening.
pitfalls: Assuming familial hyperaldosteronism will respond to glucocorticoid, as type 1 does, and delaying appropriate therapy
Interpreting normokalaemia as excluding primary aldosteronism
Proceeding to adrenalectomy without adrenal venous sampling to confirm lateralisation in bilateral disease
Not screening hypertensive relatives in an autosomal dominant condition
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on primary aldosteronism
management: Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists such as spironolactone or eplerenone as the mainstay medical therapy for bilateral adrenal disease
Unilateral adrenalectomy for a lateralised aldosterone-producing adenoma confirmed on adrenal venous sampling
Additional antihypertensive agents and potassium correction to control blood pressure and electrolytes
Note that, unlike type 1, the condition is not glucocorticoid-remediable, so dexamethasone is not therapeutic
Monitoring of blood pressure, serum potassium and cardiovascular and renal end-organ damage
Genetic counselling with CLCN2 testing and cascade family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
